transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Understood correctly, I think: your real problem isn't "how many bookings will we get", it's "how many guides does each destination need in the month after next", and you pay three times the price when you under-call and a small fee when you over-call. You'll be the one reading the number each month. Here's what I found in the export before proposing anything.

**Two things need care before any modelling.**

First, the target as worded is the wrong one. So a forecast of "bookings received in April" tells you almost nothing about how many guides you need in April; those travellers were largely booked in December and January. Forecasting the literal thing would shift your seasonality by a quarter. I plan to forecast arrivals (travellers who actually turn up) per destination per travel month, and to treat cancellations as part of the answer: 18.9% at Paris rising to 26.2% at Dubai.

Second, a warning about what your export can and cannot support. It starts on 2025-01-01, so travel months January to April 2025 are missing the bookings made before then, and months from April 2026 onward are still filling. That leaves about eleven fully observed travel months, and the booking history behind them is only fourteen months. A "machine learning model" on that is thin soil. So the honest structure is "what's already confirmed, plus the historical share still to come", with a model learning how that share moves by destination and season. I'd expect that to beat anything more complex, and I'll show it as the baseline the model must clear.

**Ways forward, one sentence each.** Forecast arrivals with a simple model: best fit for your decision, moderate effort, honest error bars. Skip the model and just use the booking curve: a defensible number this month, no accuracy claims, no learning. Forecast bookings received as your director asked: matches the request, wrong quantity for reserving guides.

The two first options you can see below are the curve report and the literal forecast. My recommendation is the arrivals forecast, and its first step is the curve anyway — so picking the curve is not a detour.

**The plan**

1. Clean and confirm the base. Drop the 12 "TEST" destination rows (your five real destinations), cast the dates, check no duplicate booking ids. Checked by row counts before and after matching.
2. Build the as-of table. For each destination and target month, snapshot only what was booked by your decision date, plus what actually turned up. Checked by confirming no booking dated after the cut-off appears in any feature.
3. Compute the curve: booked-to-date share, still-to-arrive share by destination and month, cancellation rates. Checked against the monthly totals you can eyeball.
4. Set baselines: same month last year, and booked-to-date divided by the typical arrival share. A model that can't beat these is not worth shipping.
5. Fit a simple model on arrivals, tested on the last decision cycles only, never a random split. Judge it by cost, not just error: a miss costs about triple, a spare guide costs the small fee.
6. Turn it into a reservation rule with a safety margin, and tell you which quantile to reserve given your cost ratio.

Stop when: the last two or three decision cycles are backtested, each destination has a number with a range and a cost estimate, and the model beats both baselines — otherwise you get the rule-of-thumb number and I say so plainly. If a step fails: if the signal is too thin, we ship the curve-based rule and keep the model as an experiment on next year's data.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

The bookings-received series by month: 124, 125, 112, 110, 127, 122, 94, 88, 100, 90, 104, 112, 113 — and 79 for February 2026, which is only partial (your export ends on the 24th), so I am treating February as a forecast month, not as a finished target. I am assuming the model must reach one and two months ahead, so it can serve your two-months-ahead cycle; the last three months (2025-11 to 2026-01) stay as a backtest the model never sees.

Shall I have DCLab build it on this cleaned table?

**The problem as I read it.** The board wants named groups, but the result only earns its keep if every customer lands in exactly one of three emails next quarter without your managers arguing over the middle. - `churned_next_month` cannot be a feature. It is an outcome already observed for every row, and no live customer has it; clustering on it would produce a slide that flatters the targeting and fails in the field. It belongs in naming and checking the groups afterwards, not in making them.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

Understood — and before anything else, here's how I read it: the model isn't the thing that changed. Four things did, all in the same window you noticed the complaint. So "retrain with a larger model and more features" is an answer to a question nobody has measured yet.

**What I think is really going on**

Your score ranks "likely to pay", because that's what it was trained on. Sales now reports a lead as converted when a trial *starts*. Those are different events with different rates and a lag between them, so two of your three changes (the new definition, and the fact that autumn leads simply haven't had time to reach a first payment yet) can make the top of the list *look* worse while the model behaves exactly as designed. On top of that, the marketplace is a population the model never saw in training, and the CRM switch plus two dropped form fields mean the model is being computed on new leads with inputs that are missing or mean something different from what they meant in training.

**What needs care before any work starts**

- Don't train on the blend. Old rows labelled "paid" and new rows labelled "trial started" in one dataset teaches the model whichever definition happens to dominate by date — and it learns the pre-August CRM's quirks as if they were signal. Pick one target, then derive both outcomes from event dates so nothing depends on which system reported it.
- More features is the wrong lever here. Adding inputs the pipeline no longer collects means they get imputed or silently defaulted at scoring time; offline metrics will improve and live quality will drop further.
- Your labels are touched by your own model. Sales calls the highest scores, so conversions are observed mostly for leads someone phoned. Marketplace leads that were called less will look worse than they are, and retraining on that reproduces last year's calling order rather than real lead quality. Report conversion per source and per score band, never one overall number — otherwise a segment gets scored lower, called less, and confirms its own reputation.
- Watch the clock. Trial-to-payment lag means the most recent lead months are structurally "worse" in a way that has nothing to do with the model. Compare like-matured cohorts.
- And be ready for the answer "the data can't say": if the marketplace has too few leads with matured outcomes, source effect and recency can't be separated yet.

**The plan**

1. Export and shape one row per lead: lead date, source, CRM era, the score it got at the time, trial-start date, first-payment date, and a flag per dropped field. *Check:* one row per lead, no outcome date before its lead date, counts per month.
2. Settle the target definition, and compute trial-start and first-payment separately for every lead. *Check:* the gap between the two by month — that gap alone may explain part of the complaint.
3. Measure the drift: conversion by lead-month in score deciles, split by source, plus how the score distribution moved around August. *Check:* whether ranking still holds *within* each era and each source.
4. Test whether the two lost fields were carrying the signal, by comparing the score against a version that ignores them on the period where both existed.
5. Only then choose the lever — relabel, replace features, recalibrate per source, or rebuild — and if rebuild, on a stable target, date-ordered split, validated per source on matured cohorts.
6. Put a small amount of mid-score calling in place so future labels stay unbiased.

Stop when the sales complaint is either reproduced against one fixed definition or explained by the definition change and cohort immaturity, and you can name the cause with a number. If a step fails — say the export has no score-at-scoring-time, or the marketplace rows carry no source tag — I'll tell you which question that kills and what proxy is honest, rather than guessing.

Pick one of the three above. I'd take the diagnosis, and I'd fold the table-shaping into its first step, since the numbers only mean something on a clean base. To run it I need the two exports — the old training set and every lead since. And the one thing that would change the plan most: should the score aim at trial starts, at first payments, or at trial starts with payment as a second quality target?

transcript.text: I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

[DCLab drew a dashboard above this message]

Here is what I hear you asking for, and one thing in it that has to be handled before any modelling.

**The real problem.** Management wants more approvals at a risk level they will still call safe. The model is a means, not the goal. Your goal is a decision rule you can defend: approve at rate X with a 12-month bad rate no worse than Y.

**The thing that must not be done as asked.** You have outcomes only for the ~40% your rulebook approved. So any accuracy figure computed on your 60,000 loans is a claim about people you already approve — it says nothing about the decline zone, which is exactly where all the growth lives. A model trained this way and switched on at the counter will extrapolate confidently into a region with no labels. Also keep features point-in-time: application fields and the bureau score as captured at submission, never verified income or collection flags.

**Ways to solve it.**
- *Score only where you have evidence.* Train on approvals, use the model to refine the approve zone and soften a few rules. Cheap and safe; growth stays modest, and the model still can't speak about declines.
- *Reject inference plus a controlled learning band.* Train the scorecard, then measure how many rulebook declines the model would pass, mark the score range with no outcome evidence, and approve a small random slice of borderline declines to earn real labels there. Costs a known, budgeted amount of extra defaults; it is the only route that actually delivers the growth management wants. This is the one I choose, staged: baseline first, band second.
- *Ride the bureau score.* Use the external score's own calibration as the decision and keep in-house ML as a challenger. Fastest, least defensible, little differentiation.

**The plan**
1. Fix the target in writing with management: the approval rate you want, the worst 12-month bad rate you'll accept, and roughly the margin per repaid loan against the loss per default. Checked by their sign-off, since it decides every later threshold.
2. When the export lands, specify one row per application, approvals *and* declines, with decision date, bureau score, form fields, outcome plus a maturity flag, and the rulebook reason for each decline.
3. Turn the rulebook into a measured baseline — its approval rate and its mature-cohort bad rate, and how its decline reasons map onto score bands. Checked by reproducing those numbers from your own data; this is the incumbent the model must beat.
4. Build the scorecard on approvals only, validated out-of-time on the latest untouched cohort, judged on calibration by score decile, not just ranking. Checked by stability across vintages.
5. Do the reject inference: quantify where the model would pass the rulebook's declines, name the score range with no evidence, size a randomised approval band with a loss budget, and get that budget approved.
6. Add the governance layer before counter automation: reason codes for every decline, drift and bad-rate monitoring, an override path, protected-class review with compliance.
7. Run champion/challenger against the rulebook by product or shop cohort, and switch over only where the validated bad rate holds.

Stop when: approval rate, expected bad rate and decline reasons are validated on the newest mature cohort, and management has signed both the risk ceiling and the learning-band loss budget.

If a step fails: if step 3 shows the declines were mostly identity, fraud or incomplete paperwork rather than risk, the model's job changes and we re-scope; if step 4 shows no lift over the bureau score, stop at the score, keep the rulebook, and go straight to step 5 to buy information.

I've recorded this as a full blueprint in your case file — economics, data spec, leakage traps and the pre-data task list — so we can run steps 2 to 4 the day your export arrives.

One question now, because it changes the model's target more than anything else: what bad rate will management accept at a higher approval rate, and roughly what does one repaid loan earn you against what one default costs? If the exact numbers aren't yours yet, tell me who holds them and I'll frame the plan so it forces that decision at step 1.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

1. The approval rate they want to grow to, by product and by shop cohort — not one blended number, because the growth will not be spread evenly. 2. The worst 12-month bad rate they will accept, stated as a ceiling on the *marginal* approvals (the people the rulebook declines today), not on the book overall. Blended ceilings hide the risk at the margin. 3. Two numbers that set every threshold later: what one repaid contract contributes, and what one default costs after recovery. From those comes the break-even bad rate — above it, extra approvals cost money rather than make it. I've left both blank for them to fill; I won't quote a figure you don't have. 4. Loss budget for a learning band: a small, randomised approval of borderline declines so the model earns real labels on the people it is meant to approve more of. Two rules that matter more than any modelling choice: nothing post-decision enters the features (no collection flags, no verified income, no current balance), and if the bureau changed score version, products or shop mix mid-window, the version and dates must come with it or we cannot tell drift from risk.
